ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Ghent University and Ghent University Hospital (ONZ-2022-0632).

Forty-two participants (35-65 years old) were recruited to undergo laboratory assessments of heart rate variability (HRV), baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), heart rate (HR), and mean blood pressure (MBP) at rest and during a handgrip test (i.e., a response to a physical challenge), alongside validated questionnaires assessing depression, anxiety, resilience, somatization, and emotion regulation at baseline, and after three and six months of physical training.
Forty-two participants were selected to participate in this study.
Following G*Power, to obtain this effect size (d = 0.5, with power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05), 28 participants are needed in a within-subject design.

Among the 42 participants who attended the first test day, four participants dropped out of the training program (one due to an injury, one due to lack of motivation, and two due to personal reasons).
Participants provided informed consent prior to the study.
The participants were in semi-Fowler's position with straight knees.
Participants were instructed to not perform Valsalva maneuvers.
Participants were asked to keep a pace constant and between 70 and 90 rotations per minute and were encouraged during the test to keep going.
Thirty-three participants completed at least 66% of the training.
The other three participants completed between 43 and 54% of the training.
Before each assessment session, participants were also asked to complete at-home demographic questionnaires, the GAD-7, the PHQ-9, the PHQ-15, the CERQ and the CD-RISC.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Forty-two participants were selected to participate in this study. In prior research, the effect of physical activity on ANS and psychological well-being yielded heterogeneous effectsizes ranging from small-to-medium to large (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?PhM5ON Amekran & El Hangouche, 2024; Conn, 2010; Lin, 2023). However, because a small effect size would not be clinically meaningful, we aimed for a medium effect size. Following G*Power, to obtain this effect size (d = 0.5, with power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05), 28 participants are needed in a within-subject design. We tested 50% more participants (i.e., 42), which is justified by the potentially high probability that people would drop out due to the length and level of demand of the training and our practical impossibility to recruit additional participants after the start of the study.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Physical exercise (PE) is widely recognized for its benefits on physical and mental health.

Yet its mechanisms of action on psychological outcomes remain insufficiently understood, especially regarding the role of tonic (under resting conditions) and challenge-induced response of the autonomic nervous system.
This study examined the impact of a six-month personalized, endurance exercise program on autonomic cardiovascular and psychological indices in sedentary middle-aged adults.

Forty-two participants (35-65 years old) were recruited to undergo laboratory assessments of heart rate variability (HRV), baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), heart rate (HR), and mean blood pressure (MBP) at rest and during a handgrip test (i.e., a response to a physical challenge), alongside validated questionnaires assessing depression, anxiety, resilience, somatization, and emotion regulation at baseline, and after three and six months of physical training.

Results revealed significant improvements in autonomic cardiovascular function with a specific temporal pattern: HR decreased and BRS increased after three months and remained stable at six months, while HRV and MBP improved only after six months.
These effects were all observed at the tonic level, with the training not affecting the cardiovascular response to the handgrip test.
Unexpectedly, no stable effect was found on psychological variables after three or six months of personalized PE.
In addition, changes in cardiovascular markers did not predict improvements in psychological outcomes.

This study reinforces long-term PE programs as a scalable means to enhance cardiovascular and autonomic health, but yields limited evidence that such autonomic gains are associated with meaningful psychological improvements.

A substantial body of research indicates that physical exercise (PE), defined as "a subset of physical activity that is planned, structured and repetitive, and has as a final or an intermediate objective the improvement or maintenance of physical fitness" (Caspersen et al., 1985), has significant health benefits across the lifespan (Penedo & Dahn, 2005).

text.text: Beyond these well-documented benefits, PE represents a scalable and cost-effective intervention with minimal adverse effects.

One proposed mechanism involves the autonomic nervous system (ANS).

Within this context, physical challenges may provide important insights into the effects of PE on ANS regulation and its implications for mental health.

Physical challenges activate the autonomic cardiovascular system in a manner similar to psychosocial or emotional stressors, characterized by parasympathetic withdrawal and increased cardiac sympathetic activity (e.g., Michael et al., 2017).

text.formatted: In prior research, the effect of physical activity on ANS and psychological well-being yielded heterogeneous effectsizes ranging from small-to-medium to large (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?PhM5ON">e.g.,</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Amekran & El Hangouche, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Conn, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lin, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, because a small effect size would not be clinically meaningful, we aimed for a medium effect size.
Following G*Power, to obtain this effect size (d = 0.5, with power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05), 28 participants are needed in a within-subject design.

We tested 50% more participants (i.e., 42), which is justified by the potentially high probability that people would drop out due to the length and level of demand of the training and our practical impossibility to recruit additional participants after the start of the study.

Inclusion criteria were: being between 35 and 65 years old, having no established medical conditions (e.g., diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, neural conditions were excluded while people with blood sugar imbalance, abnormal cholesterol levels, slightly elevated blood pressure or obesity were accepted) and not using medication that could impact the epigenetic clock and/or inhibit training response (e.g., metformin and antihistamines).
The recruitment targeted individuals with physically inactive lifestyles assessed by daily activity levels, sedentary behavior, and lack of participation in sports.

From 151 candidates, 42 were selected, ensuring equal representation of males and females and an approximately even distribution across the age groups: 35-39, 40-44, 45-49, 50-54, 55-59, and 60-65 years.
The final sample included in this study was of 36 participants (Mage = 48,40, SDage = 8,58, 52,78% females).

Among the 42 participants who attended the first test day, four participants dropped out of the training program (one due to an injury, one due to lack of motivation, and two due to personal reasons).
One participant continued in the study but did not complete the training due to personal reasons, and cardiovascular data from one participant is missing due to problems with the signal.

text.text: This study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Ghent University and Ghent University Hospital (ONZ-2022-0632).
Participants provided informed consent prior to the study.
Cardiovascular variables were recorded and analyzed through the Biopac MP160 system and Biopac Acqknowledge software 4.3 (Biopac Systems Inc., USA).
The participants were in semi-Fowler's position with straight knees.
Electrocardiography (ECG) was recorded through three electrodes attached under the right and left clavicles and on the left lower rib, at 1000 Hz.
Continuous blood pressure was acquired through a CNAP 500® system (CNSystems Medizintechnik AG) at 100 Hz.
The cuff and the finger sensor were put on the left arm of the participant.
ECG and blood pressure signals were preprossed using custom flexible algorithms to detect R-R intervals and beat-to-beat systolic and diastolic peaks.
Possible artefacts were checked by visual inspection and corrected by linear interpolation when present (Reyes del Paso et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Possible artefacts were checked by visual inspection and corrected by linear interpolation when present (Reyes del <ref type="bibr">Paso et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As the main outcome of HRV, we used the root mean square of successive R-R interval differences (RMSSD), a time-domain index that is relatively free of respiratory influence (Laborde et al., 2017).
text.formatted: As the main outcome of HRV, we used the root mean square of successive R-R interval differences (RMSSD), a time-domain index that is relatively free of respiratory influence <ref type="bibr">(Laborde et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As exploratory analyses, we also report the effect of the training on the high-frequency HRV (HF), and the low-frequency HRV (LF), two frequency-domain indices.
The HF and LF indices were computed by means of Fast-Fourier transformations in the frequency ranges of 0.15-0.40Hz and 0.04-0.15Hz by using the Kubios software (Niskanen et al., 2004).
text.formatted: The HF and LF indices were computed by means of Fast-Fourier transformations in the frequency ranges of 0.15-0.40Hz and 0.04-0.15Hz by using the Kubios software <ref type="bibr">(Niskanen et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: As indices of baroreflex function, we calculated the baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), which measures the magnitude of change in inter-beat interval (IBI) per unit of change in systolic blood pressure (SBP), and the Baroreflex Effectiveness Index (BEI), which indicates the proportion of progressive changes in SBP (SBP ramps) followed by the expected IBI reflex modulation (Di Rienzo et al., 2001; Reyes del Paso et al., 2017).
text.formatted: As indices of baroreflex function, we calculated the baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), which measures the magnitude of change in inter-beat interval (IBI) per unit of change in systolic blood pressure (SBP), and the Baroreflex Effectiveness Index (BEI), which indicates the proportion of progressive changes in SBP (SBP ramps) followed by the expected IBI reflex modulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Di Rienzo et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Reyes del Paso et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Both BRS and BEI were quantified through the spontaneous sequence method in the time domain.
The minimal required cardiac cycles was set at 3, the IBI change threshold at 1 millisecond and the SBP at 1mmHg.

The spontaneous sequence method locates sequences of 3 to 6 consecutive cardiac cycles in which SBP increases ("up" sequences) are accompanied by increases in IBI and those in which SBP decreases ("down" sequences) are accompanied by IBI decreases.
Correlation between SBP and IBI values within the sequence has to be greater than .85 to consider it as a reflex sequence.
When one of these reflex sequences was detected, a regression line was computed across its SBP-IBI values.
BRS is indexed by the slope of the regression line, as the change in IBI per unit of change in SBP (ms/mmHg).
The BEI is calculated as the ratio between the number of SBP ramps followed by reflex changes in IBI and the total number of SBP ramps (reflex and non-reflex) (Reyes del Paso et al., 2017).
The GAD-7 (Donker et al., 2011; Spitzer et al., 2006) consists of 7 items about anxiety symptoms experienced in the last two weeks.
text.formatted: The GAD-7 <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Donker et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Spitzer et al., 2006)</ref> consists of 7 items about anxiety symptoms experienced in the last two weeks.

text.text: Participants answered on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from0 = not at all to3 = almost every day.
The total score (between 0 and 21) was calculated by summing all individual items, with higher scores indicating higher levels of anxiety.
In the current study, the GAD-7 showed Cronbach's alpha of 0.9, 0.88 and 0.69 for GAD-7 related to T1, T2 and T3, respectively.

The CERQ (Garnefski et al., 2001) consists of 36 items assessing nine cognitive emotion regulation strategies typically used after negative events: self-blame, acceptance, rumination, positive refocusing, refocus on planning, positive reappraisal, putting into perspective, catastrophizing, and blaming others.
text.formatted: The CERQ <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Garnefski et al., 2001</ref>) consists of 36 items assessing nine cognitive emotion regulation strategies typically used after negative events: self-blame, acceptance, rumination, positive refocusing, refocus on planning, positive reappraisal, putting into perspective, catastrophizing, and blaming others.

text.text: Participants responded on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 ((almost) never) to 5 ((almost) always).

Scores for each of the nine subscales (between 4 and 20) were computed by averaging the four corresponding items, with higher scores indicating greater use of the respective emotion regulation strategy.
In the current study, all subscales showed a Cronbach's alpha of 0.67 or higher for the three evaluation periods.
The grip test (Chirinos et al., 2020) was performed using an E-LINK H500 Hand Kit hand grip dynamometer (Biometrics Ltd., Gwent, UK).
text.formatted: The grip test <ref type="bibr">(Chirinos et al., 2020)</ref> was performed using an E-LINK H500 Hand Kit hand grip dynamometer (Biometrics Ltd., Gwent, UK).

text.text: First, to determine their maximal strength, the participants gripped twice the hand grip as hard as possible.
The highest value was used as a reference value.

In a second phase, the participants played an interactive computer game where they had to keep a ball between two lines by gripping the hand grip dynamometer at approximately 25% of their maximal strength.
Participants were instructed to not perform Valsalva maneuvers.
They were asked to let the experimenter know when they thought they would have difficulty holding out for one more minute.
When they did, the experimenter performed a pulse wave velocity measurement.
Once it was completed, participants released the hand grip dynamometer.
A single experimenter (E.R.R., an experienced cardiologist) performed the handgrip assessment for all the participants.
To personalize the program intensity, participants performed a VO₂max test during each lab session.

The VO₂max test consisted of an incremental step exercise on a cycle ergometer Cyclus 2, RBM Elektronik-automation GmbH, Leipzig, Germany), starting at 60W with an increase of 40 Watt per 5 min for the men and 30 Watt per 5 min for the women.
Participants were asked to keep a pace constant and between 70 and 90 rotations per minute and were encouraged during the test to keep going.
The test stopped when the participant could no longer bicycle.

During the test, pulmonary gas exchange (Cosmed quark cpet system, Omnia Software version 1.6.10, Benelux, Nieuwegein, The Netherlands) and blood lactate concentration (through a capillary blood sample from the earlobe; Lactate Pro 2, Arkray, Kyoto, JAPAN) were recorded.

We then computed the VO2max (i.e., highest 30-seconds average VO2), the aerobic threshold (i.e., when the lactate had increased by 0.5 mmol/L from baseline) and the anaerobic threshold (using the Dmax method).
Those values were used to determine the training zone of each participant and hence personalize the training program, which was aimed at increasing the VO2max.
The training was supervised by our exercise scientists and monitored by personal coaches (from Golazo Energy, https://energy.golazo.com/) during biweekly online meetings with the participants.
text.formatted: The training was supervised by our exercise scientists and monitored by personal coaches (from Golazo Energy, <ref type="url" target="https://energy.golazo.com/">https://energy.golazo.com</ref>) during biweekly online meetings with the participants.

text.text: The training schedule was discussed between the participant and the coach, aiming to have three training sessions, for a total of approximately 3h30 to 7h of sport per week.

Participants also received a wearable clock (Garmin Forerunner 255, Garmin Ltd., Olathe, KS, USA) so that their training sessions and some basic health variables such as sleep duration and HRV during the night could be monitored.
They also attended three workshops on bike usage, nutrition and sleep.

Following the World Health Organization recommendations (≥150 min/week, ~65 hours over 26 weeks), successful completion was determined at the end of the intervention, before further data analysis, as having more than 66% adherence to the training program based on Garmin-measured training time.
Thirty-three participants completed at least 66% of the training.
The other three participants completed between 43 and 54% of the training.
Given that the conclusions of the study are the same if those participants completing less than 66% of the training are excluded from the analyses, we report the results with the entire sample.
Participants came to the lab before starting the training program, and at 3 and 6 months after the beginning of the program for an assessment session.
Between sessions, they performed the training program independently by cycling at locations of their choice.
Before each assessment session, participants were also asked to complete at-home demographic questionnaires, the GAD-7, the PHQ-9, the PHQ-15, the CERQ and the CD-RISC.
If they had not done so, they filled them in upon arrival at the lab.

For the three assessment sessions, we asked participants to not change their habits the day before (e.g., eat and sleep during their regular hours, have their usual breakfast/lunch) with three exceptions: they were asked to (1) refrain from physical exercise at least 24h before the appointment, (2) not eat immediately before the session (3) reduce their consumption of alcohol the day before the study and, if possible, not drink alcohol the night before.
Physiological data analyzed in this study were collected during the recording of ECG and blood pressure at rest and during a handgrip test.
When entering the room, the participants underwent a measurement of carotid artery-sternum-femoral artery and the maximal grip strength test.

Then, after placing equipment on the participants and calibrating, we ask them to be still for 5 minutes for the baseline recording (resting period) and then, to perform the handgrip test while the ECG and continuous blood pressure were recorded.
The pulse wave velocity measurement was carried out before and after the handgrip test.

The same day of the assessment session, participants underwent a body composition determination by DEXA-scan, a medical sport examination, a blood sampling, a V02max test, and a consultation session with a discussion of the results.
The data reported in this study correspond to the ECG and continuous blood pressure recorded at rest and during the handgrip test.
All data were analyzed in R 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2024) in conjunction with Rstudio 2024.09.1+394.
Linear mixed effects regressions (LMER) were used to investigate the effect of training on cardiovascular and psychological variables.
For cardiovascular variables (RMSSD, HF, LF, HR, MBP, BRS, and BEI), Time (Baseline, 3 months, and 6 months) and Condition (Resting, Grip Test) were used as fixed factors.
For questionnaires (GAD, CD-RISC, PHQ-15, PHQ-9, and CERQ subscales), Time (Baseline, 3 months, and 6 months) was used as a fixed factor.
In all these models, we included random intercepts for subjects, and we included the percentage of completed training as covariate.
P-values are provided using the Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom approximation.
To decompose interaction effects, Tukey adjusted pairwise comparisons were carried out using the 'emmeans' package (Lenth & Lenth, 2018).

text.text: We used LMER models to investigate whether changes in cardiovascular markers predict changes in psychological factors.
As the dependent variable, we included the score on GAD, PHQ9, PHQ15, CDRISC, or the Others-blame subscale from the CERQ.

As independent variables, we included Time (3 months, 6 months), change in RMSSD, HR, MBP, or BRS (calculated as the change from baseline to 3 and 6 months), the percentage of training achieved by the participant, and baseline scores on the questionnaires.

Given that the results reported above indicate that the effect of training is specific for baseline cardiovascular activity, and not for reactivity (i.e., the factor Time was statistically significant, but the interaction between Time and Condition was not significant in all models), we performed these models including only the resting period.
In all these models, the change in cardiovascular markers did not predict the score on GAD, PHQ9, PHQ15, CDRISC and Self-Blame (all p>0.068).

text.text: In this study we investigated the effect of a personalized supervised six-month endurance PE program on cardiovascular markers of ANS regulation and psychological indices of mental health in a group of sedentary middle-aged individuals.
Regarding cardiovascular ANS indices, we observed a decrease in HR and an increase in BRS after three months of training, and the change remained stable after six months of training.
The effects of training on HRV (as measured by RMSSD), and MBP were observed only after six months of training, but not yet after three months.
Importantly, these effects were specific for tonic autonomic cardiovascular activity, and no change in the cardiovascular reactivity to the handgrip test was observed.

Frequency-domain HRV indices (HF and LF) increased after six months of training, but the change was not statistically significant, possibly reflecting their greater variability relative to time-domain measures such as RMSSD.
The main effects on cardiovascular markers remain the same even after controlling for changes in handgrip strength.

Regarding psychological indices, we observed a decrease in the use of other-blaming ("putting the blame for what you have experienced on the environment or another person"; Garnefski & Kraaij, 2007, pp 141-142) as an emotion regulation strategy after three months of training.
text.formatted: Regarding psychological indices, we observed a decrease in the use of other-blaming ("putting the blame for what you have experienced on the environment or another person"; <ref type="bibr">Garnefski & Kraaij, 2007, pp 141-142)</ref> as an emotion regulation strategy after three months of training.

text.text: However, this change did not stabilize and returned to baseline levels after six months of training.

None of the other psychological constructs (self-reported depression symptoms, anxiety, resilience, somatization, and other emotion regulation strategies) changed after three or six months of training.
Importantly, our results also showed that the changes in cardiovascular markers of ANS regulation do not translate into psychological improvements.
Our findings demonstrate that a supervised, personalized six-month exercise intervention improved tonic cardiovascular regulation in sedentary middle-aged adults.
Specifically, participants exhibited higher HRV (RMSSD), higher BRS, and lower HR and MBP both at rest and during handgrip performance.
However, training did not modify cardiovascular reactivity to the handgrip test.
Improvements in BRS were observed for both "up" and "down" sequences, indicating enhanced vagal activation and withdrawal (Martín-Vázquez & Reyes del Paso, 2010; Reyes del Paso et al., 2017).

text.text: Together, our findings reinforce the role of structured PE programs as an effective strategy for enhancing tonic autonomic regulation (e.g., Debi et al., 2019; Fu & Levine, 2013; Martín-Vázquez & Reyes del Paso, 2010; Navarro-Lomas et al., 2022; Reyes del Paso et al., 2017; Soares-Miranda et al., 2012; Ueno & Moritani, 2003) and physical health, and hence promoting physiological resilience to cardiovascular disorders in adults.

text.text: It is important to note that improvements in BRS and HR emerged after three months, whereas RMSSD and MBP changed only after six months.

This novel result on the temporal pattern of PE-induced changes in ANS indicates that exercise first influences baroreflex functioning, followed by longer-term adaptations in vagal modulation and vascular regulation.
Thus, sustained interventions appear necessary to obtain clinically meaningful cardiovascular benefits in sedentary individuals.

Although the personalized physical exercise (PE) training enhanced vagal activity and baroreflex function, two markers of autonomic regulation associated with stress-related mental disorders (Broadley et al., 2005; Chalmers et al., 2014; Perna et al., 2020), it did not affect selfreported depression, anxiety, resilience, or somatization.

text.text: Changes in autonomic cardiovascular activity were also unrelated to psychological outcomes.
The only psychological effect was a reduced tendency to blame others, which was present after three months but not after six months of training.

These findings are consistent with a recent systematic review showing small and heterogeneous effects of physical activity interventions on repetitive thinking, a major risk factor for depression and anxiety, in healthy adults (Wang et al., 2025).

text.text: Although PE improved tonic cardiovascular autonomic activity both at rest and during the handgrip test, it did not alter the magnitude of the phasic response.
This suggests that improving tonic autonomic regulation alone may be insufficient to influence mental well-being.

Supporting this interpretation, recent large-scale studies found that resting HRV was unrelated to depression and rumination despite being associated with physical activity (Li et al., 2024 (Li et al., , 2026)).

text.text: Together, our findings indicate that PE-related increases in resting autonomic cardiovascular control do not necessarily lead to improvements on mental health and well-being in sedentary healthy adults, and contradict the link between resting HRV and mental health proposed by the Neurovisceral Integration Model (Thayer and Lane, 2009).

text.text: Theoretical and empirical evidence suggests that exaggerated physiological reactions to stressors are associated with reduced mental health and well-being (e.g., Vanderhasselt et al., 2025).

text.text: In this context, it is possible that PE does not translate into psychological benefits unless autonomic reactivity to stressors is also modified.
According to the cross-stressor adaptation hypothesis (Sothmann et al., 1996), PE may improve well-being by enhancing autonomic regulation responses to challenges.

text.text: However, it is important to note that evidence supporting this hypothesis is generally modest and largely based on cross-sectional research (Forcier et al., 2006; Jackson & Dishman, 2006; Mücke et al., 2018).

text.text: For example, a recent study in untrained individuals showed that a 6-month aerobic exercise intervention did not alter cardiovascular (heart rate and blood pressure) or endocrine (cortisol and ACTH) responses to acute psychosocial stress compared to a non-training control group (Ardvison et al., 2020).

text.text: Notably, both groups exhibited attenuated stress responses over time, suggesting habituation to the stress paradigm.

To minimize habituation effects and reduce interindividual variability in emotional responses to psychosocial stress tasks, the present study employed a standardized physical challenge, which activate the autonomic cardiovascular system in a manner similar to psychosocial or emotional stressors (i.e., decrease in parasympathetic control and increased cardiac sympathetic activity) and is less affected by habituation in longitudinal designs.

Also, important in the context of this study, previous studies have shown a link between the autonomic response to physical challenges and stress-related disorders such as depression and anxiety (Guinjoan et al., 1997; Udupa et al., 2007; Bylsma et sl., 2015; Asbrand et al., 2017).

text.text: Nevertheless, no PE-related effects on autonomic cardiovascular responses were observed.

Although it remains important to determine whether the present intervention influences autonomic responses to psychosocial stress specifically, our findings add to the growing body of evidence suggesting small or null effects of aerobic PE interventions on autonomic cardiovascular reactivity to challenges.

Taken together, although PE has been consistently associated with improvements in mental well-being, further research is needed to determine under which conditions PE may strengthen adaptive autonomic responses to challenges and whether such changes mediate its beneficial effects on mental health.
For instance, the training program in this study was largely technical and performance-oriented, conducted individually, and emphasized physiological improvement with limited social interaction.

Recent theoretical work suggests that social connection and support, along with lifestyle factors (including physical activity) constitute central components of mental well-being and that may influence stress regulation (Vanderhasselt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent theoretical work suggests that social connection and support, along with lifestyle factors (including physical activity) constitute central components of mental well-being and that may influence stress regulation <ref type="bibr">(Vanderhasselt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, future research should investigate whether exercise programs that incorporate socially enjoyable and engaging elements may lead to stronger psychological benefits via enhancing stress regulation.

Although this study has multiple strengths, including the length of the training and the closely monitored, objectively personalized PE program, some methodological aspects should be considered when interpreting our results.

First, although the selected individuals were physically inactive, which has been associated with lower HRV and poorer mental health, the participation in this study necessitated motivation, physical effort, engagement and regular talk with the coach for a long period.
As a result, we may have recruited individuals who, despite being physically inactive, may have greater psychological resources.
Future studies should focus on participants who are not only inactive but also show high symptoms of anxiety and depression.
Second, we used a pre-post design without a control group.
Thus, we cannot exclude the possibility that the effects observed are attributable to other uncontrolled factors.
Nevertheless, the prospective nature of the study provides important evidence that could have not been obtained in cross-sectional designs.
Still, future studies comparing PE with a control group are needed to replicate these findings.

In conclusion, our findings show that a 6-months sport training can improve tonic BRS, HR, HRV, and MBP, adding further evidence of its potential as a scalable way to improve tonic cardiovascular ANS activity.

However, it also showed no effect on depression, anxiety, or somatic symptoms, resilience and emotion regulation nor did changes in cardiovascular ANS indices predict changes in psychological variables.

These null findings therefore do not support theoretical models suggesting that gains in tonic autonomic regulation are associated with improved regulation of stress-related psychological symptoms and mental well-being, asking for more research causally modulating ANS to assess its impact on mental well-being.
